result.summary: Pausanias describes how the Olympic programme changed over time: the boys' pentathlum, the chariot race and the trotting race were dropped, and the order of events was rearranged. He then traces how the number of Olympic umpires (Hellanodikai) changed from Iphitus alone to ten.

scenes.title: Discontinued Olympic contests
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists contests the Eleans abolished: the boys' pentathlum, the mule chariot race and the trotting race. He names early winners and describes the trotting race.

scenes.title: Order of the games
scenes.summary: He explains the programme set in the 77th Olympiad, after earlier crowding pushed the pancratium into the night, when Callias won.

scenes.title: Changing number of umpires
scenes.summary: He traces the umpires from Iphitus alone, to Oxylus's descendants, two chosen by lot, then nine, ten, twelve, eight and finally ten again.

analysis.text: The passage shows the Olympic Games as an evolving institution, with events added, dropped and rescheduled by the Eleans.
Pausanias is concerned with antiquarian detail and Elean custom, and he records the Eleans' dislike of horses and the growth of their administration.

fun_facts.text: Umpires' numbers tied to Elis's tribes, so losing territory to the Arcadians reduced the tribes and the umpires to eight.

language_notes.text: "Contests" here means athletic events in the Olympic programme; "Elis" is the region that administered the games.
The pentathlum was the five-event contest (running, jumping, discus, javelin, wrestling). The crown of wild olive was the Olympic victor's prize.
"The former" and "the latter" are muddled here: the text means the mule chariot race (established 70th) and the trotting race (71st), though the mule race is not named.
"Professional riders" translates the Greek word for riders of the saddle-horse (keletizontes) in Pausanias' own day; they rode stallions and wore racing colours.
Pancratiasts were competitors in the pancratium, a brutal combination of boxing and wrestling.
"Umpires" translates Hellanodicae, the Elean judges of the Games; "in vogue" means in current use.
Oxylus was the legendary Aetolian king of Elis; Iphitus is the traditional reviver of the Olympic Games.
"Hard pressed by the Arcadians" refers to wars in which Arcadia took Elean border territory, reducing the number of tribes.

context_notes.text: Dyme was a city of Achaia in the northern Peloponnese; Thessaly lay in northern Greece.
Callias of Athens is recorded as a pancratium victor; the late-night finish shows the programme's crowding.
The Eleans were divided into twelve tribes, so each tribe supplied one umpire.

literary_notes.text: The parenthesis gives the Eleans a trait, dislike of horses, and offers it as the reason for their mule-yoking practice.
The picture of wrestlers competing only after dark vividly conveys how overloaded the programme had become.
The closing note on the present-day number gives the list a sense of completion and shows the author's antiquarian method.
